{{Short description|Number that is the product of factorials}}
[[File:Tree with 480 symmetries.svg|thumb|upright=1.2|A tree that (as an abstract [[graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]]) has 480 symmetries (automorphisms). There are 2 ways of permuting the two children of the upper left vertex, 2 ways of permuting the two children of the upper middle vertex, and 5! = 120 ways of permuting the five children of the upper right vertex, for 2 · 2 · 120 = 480 symmetries altogether.]]
In [[mathematics]], the '''Jordan–Pólya numbers''' are the numbers that can be obtained by multiplying together one or more [[factorial]]s, not required to be distinct from each other. For instance, <math>480</math> is a Jordan–Pólya number because {{nowrap|<math>480=2!\cdot 2!\cdot5!</math>.}} Every [[tree (graph theory)|tree]] has a number of [[graph automorphism|symmetries]] that is a Jordan–Pólya number, and every Jordan–Pólya number arises in this way as the [[Order (group theory)|order]] of an [[automorphism group]] of a tree. These numbers are named after [[Camille Jordan]] and [[George Pólya]], who both wrote about them in the context of symmetries of trees.{{r|jordan|polya}}

These numbers grow more quickly than [[polynomial]]s but more slowly than [[exponential function|exponentials]]. As well as in the symmetries of trees, they arise as the numbers of [[transitive orientation]]s of [[comparability graph]]s{{r|golumbic}} and in the problem of finding factorials that can be represented as products of smaller factorials.

==Sequence and growth rate==
The [[integer sequence|sequence]] of Jordan–Pólya numbers begins:{{r|oeis}}
{{bi|left=1.6|1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 36, 48, 64, 72, 96, 120, 128, 144, 192, 216, 240, 256, ... {{OEIS|A001013}}}}
They form the smallest [[multiplicatively closed set]] containing all of the factorials.

The <math>n</math>th Jordan–Pólya number grows more quickly than any polynomial of <math>n</math>, but more slowly than any exponential function of <math>n</math>. More precisely, for every <math>\varepsilon>0</math>, and every sufficiently large <math>x</math> (depending on <math>\varepsilon</math>), the number <math>J(x)</math> of Jordan–Pólya numbers up to <math>x</math> obeys the [[inequality (mathematics)|inequalities]]{{r|ddrv}}
<math display=block>
\exp\frac{(2-\varepsilon)\sqrt{\log x}}{\log\log x} < J(x) <
\exp\frac{(4+\varepsilon)\sqrt{\log x}\log\log\log x}{\log\log x}.</math>

==Factorials that are products of smaller factorials==
Every Jordan–Pólya number <math>n</math>, except 2, has the property that its factorial <math>n!</math> can be written as a product of smaller factorials. This can be done simply by expanding <math>n!=n\cdot(n-1)!</math> and then replacing <math>n</math> in this product by its representation as a product of factorials. It is [[conjecture]]d, but [[mathematical proof|unproven]], that the only numbers <math>n</math> whose factorial <math>n!</math> equals a product of smaller factorials are the Jordan–Pólya numbers (except 2) and the two exceptional numbers 9 and 10, for which <math>9!=2!\cdot3!\cdot3!\cdot7!</math> and <math>10!=6!\cdot7!=3!\cdot5!\cdot7!</math>. The only other known representation of a factorial as a product of smaller factorials, not obtained by replacing <math>n</math> in the product expansion of <math>n!</math>, is <math>16!=2!\cdot5!\cdot14!</math>, but as <math>16</math> is itself a Jordan–Pólya number, it also has the representation <math>16!=2!^4\cdot 15!</math>.{{r|oeis|guy}}
